I couldn't finish this research. My search and fetch allowance ran out early, after only a few lookups, so I couldn't read the verse-by-verse sources for verses 148–176: Gill, Ellicott, the Pulpit Commentary, Spurgeon, Precept Austin, or the Enduring Word section on these verses. I also found nothing for the Catholic, Orthodox, modern-scholarship or popular-teaching sections. The notes below cover only what I actually read. Most verses aren't covered.

**Whole psalm (background)**
- The psalm doesn't name its author. Older commentators almost all said David wrote it over his lifetime, while some modern ones date it after the exile, around the time of Ezra or Nehemiah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- Guzik (Enduring Word) thinks it was probably written over time and compiled later. In his picture it is like a string of pearls, each of equal but separate value, rather than a chain of linked thoughts. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- It is an acrostic: 22 sections of 8 verses, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Lamentations 3 is the closest parallel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- Guzik's titles for the sections in this passage: Resh (153–160) "Revival According to the Word of God", Shin (161–168) "In Awe of God's Word", Tau (169–176) "Sought by God and His Word". These come from a video list on the page; the written notes for these sections didn't load. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/

**v. 149:**
- John Wesley (Methodist) reads "according to thy judgment" as meaning according to God's word. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/psalms/119-149.html
- The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary (1876) treats God's loving-kindness here as what entitles anyone to pray at all. If God weren't gracious, we would have no right to approach his majesty. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/psalms/119-149.html

**v. 150:**
- Wesley says "draw nigh" means the enemies are close to the psalmist and ready to seize him. "Far from thy law" means they have thrown off every thought of God's law. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/psalms-119.html

**v. 152:**
- Wesley takes "of old" to mean the psalmist knew this from long experience. "Founded them for ever" means God set his testimonies on foundations that last forever. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/reb/psalms/119-152.html

**v. 165:**
- Wesley notes that "offend" (KJV) literally means they will have no stumbling-block to trip over and fall into harm. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/esv/psalms/119-165.html
- The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary says people lose their peace when they trip over obstacles. Those who love God's law have no fear of these stumbling-blocks and aren't hurt by them, so their peace is great, not just ordinary. It ties this to Christ defeating the one who held the power of death. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/esv/psalms/119-165.html
- The Sermon Bible Commentary (1888) says loving God's law is a mature attainment. Without assurance of pardon through Christ's blood, the law would only bring terror. Such people don't stumble for two reasons: they trust God's justice to settle the unfair share of good and evil at the final judgment, and they hold loosely to this world because their hearts are set on heaven. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/esv/psalms/119-165.html

**v. 175:**
- Wesley takes "thy judgments" to mean God's word or testimonies, which he calls the only ground for hoping in God's help. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/psalms-119.html

**Not found:** verses 148, 151, 153–164, 166–174 and 176. I also have no differing Protestant positions (Wesley is the only tradition-specific voice above) and no Catholic, Orthodox, modern-scholarship or prosperity/word-of-faith/hyper-grace material for any verse.

To fill the gaps in a new session, the most useful pages would be:
- Enduring Word's separate Resh, Shin and Tau pages
- the Bible Hub or StudyLight verse pages for each verse (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit, Barnes, Spurgeon)
- Precept Austin's Psalm 119 notes
- the NET Bible notes
- Augustine's exposition on New Advent, where the psalm is numbered 118 because of the Latin numbering
